category: Application Builder, LiveLink, API & command line
description: How COMSOL Multiphysics 6.3 is driven from outside the Model Builder: the Application Builder (Form Editor, Method Editor, Declarations, Events, Model Methods, Test Application) for turning a model into a custom app, the COMSOL API for Java that every GUI action maps onto, LiveLink for MATLAB and the community MPh package for Python, and the command-line programs that run models, servers and compilers headless. The same object model underlies all of them, so a workflow recorded in the GUI can be replayed from Java, MATLAB, Python or a batch script. Related interfacing products - LiveLink for Excel and Simulink, the LiveLink CAD products for SOLIDWORKS, Inventor, AutoCAD, Revit, PTC Creo Parametric and Solid Edge, and the CAD/ECAD Import and Design Modules - attach to the same model object.

tools.name: Form Editor
tools.description: The drag-and-drop designer for an application's user interface. You place form objects - input fields, buttons, sliders, knobs, checkboxes, combo boxes, graphics windows, tables, text labels, images and data display fields - on a form and bind each one to a model parameter, a declared variable or a method. No programming is required for the layout itself; the binding is what makes an end user's edit change the underlying model. Forms can be arranged as a single window or as a set of subwindows and dialog forms.
tools.usage: Home ribbon > Application Builder, then select a form under Applications > <app> > Forms, or double-click a form object to edit it

parameters.name: Source
parameters.description: What a form object reads and writes: a model parameter (comp1.param), a declared scalar or array, or a results table.

parameters.name: Layout mode
parameters.description: Sketch (grid) or Grid layout, controlling how objects reflow when the window is resized.

parameters.name: Events
parameters.description: The method (if any) that runs when the object's value changes or a button is clicked.

parameters.name: Appearance
parameters.description: Label, tooltip, units, icon, colour, state (enabled/visible) and conditional activation.

tools.example:
Steps to bind an input field to a model parameter:
1. Home > Application Builder.
2. Right-click Forms > New Form, and drag an Input Field onto the canvas.
3. In the Settings window click Source > Model > Global Definitions > Parameters, pick L.
4. Drag a Button next to it, set Choose Commands to Run > Study 1 > Compute Study.
5. Click Test Application to try it, then File > Save As to save the .mph containing the app.
tools.notes: The Main Window editor is a sibling of the Form Editor: it designs the app's menus, ribbon tabs, toolbars and subwindow layout, plus the application title, icon, window size and About dialog. A form object bound to a parameter only takes effect once the model is rebuilt or re-solved, so most apps pair inputs with a Compute button or a method.

tools.name: Method Editor
tools.description: A full Java editor inside COMSOL for writing the code behind an application: methods that read form inputs, change the model, run studies, evaluate results, write files and update the interface. It supports Java 11 with syntax highlighting and code completion over the COMSOL API, and provides built-in helper methods such as message(), alert(), confirm(), readCSVFile(), readMatrixFromFile() and saveApplicationCopyAs(). Use it whenever the application needs logic that form bindings alone cannot express.
tools.usage: Application Builder > Methods > right-click > New Method (or Developer ribbon > New Method); double-click a method to open the Method Editor

parameters.name: Method name
parameters.description: Identifier used to call the method from a button, an event or another method.

parameters.name: Inputs / Output
parameters.description: Optional typed arguments and return value declared in the method's Settings window.

parameters.name: Record Code
parameters.description: Records GUI actions in the Model Builder straight into the method body - the fastest way to learn the API calls for a node.

parameters.name: Java Shell
parameters.description: Interactive prompt (added in 6.3) for running COMSOL API Java snippets against the loaded model without creating a method first.

tools.notes: COMSOL 6.3 added Java 11 support with code completion, delimiter options for readCSVFile/readMatrixFromFile/readStringMatrixFromFile, saveApplicationCopyAs, and an interactive Java Shell window. Methods stored in an application are only reachable inside that application; use Model Methods when you want code callable from an ordinary model and from batch.

tools.name: Model Methods
tools.description: Java methods stored in an ordinary .mph model rather than in an application, callable from the Developer ribbon, from other methods, from a Method Call study step, and from the command line with comsol batch -methodcall. They are the standard way to automate repetitive modelling work - building geometry from a table, looping over designs, post-processing to a file - without leaving COMSOL or writing an external script. A Method Call node under Study lets a method run as part of the solve sequence.
tools.usage: Developer ribbon > New Method (creates a Model Method); run it with Developer > Run Method, or headless with `comsol batch -inputfile m.mph -methodcall <methodname>`

parameters.name: Method name
parameters.description: The name passed to -methodcall and used by Method Call study steps.

parameters.name: Inputs / Output
parameters.description: Typed arguments and return type, declared in the method Settings window.

parameters.name: model
parameters.description: The implicit variable bound to the current model object inside the method body.

parameters.name: Method Call (study step)
parameters.description: Study node that executes a model method at a chosen point in the solve sequence.

tools.example:
# Run a model method headless, overriding two parameters, without re-saving the model
comsolbatch -inputfile my_file.mph -pname tbb,Vtot -plist "1[cm]","10[mV]" -methodcall my_method -nosave
tools.notes: Model methods can call MATLAB functions when LiveLink for MATLAB is licensed, and they can read and write files, which makes them a convenient glue layer for digital-twin and data-driven workflows. Because they execute Java in the COMSOL process, a badly behaved method can hang a batch job - guard long loops and check for null before dereferencing model nodes.

tools.name: Declarations
tools.description: The branch of an application that declares its own variables, separate from the model's parameters. You add Scalar declarations (string, Boolean, integer, double), Array 1D and Array 2D declarations of the same four types, plus Choice List, File, File Type, Unit Set, Graphics Data and Shortcuts nodes. Form objects bind to these declarations, and methods read and write them, so they act as the application's state: current mode, last opened file, allowed material list, table of load cases.
tools.usage: Application Builder > Declarations > right-click, or use the Declarations section of the Application Builder ribbon (Scalar / Array 1D / Array 2D / More Declarations)

parameters.name: Scalar
parameters.description: String, Boolean, Integer or Double single values.

parameters.name: Array 1D / Array 2D
parameters.description: Vectors and matrices of string, Boolean, integer or double values - used to back tables and list boxes.

parameters.name: Choice List
parameters.description: Named list of allowed value/display-name pairs that drives combo boxes and radio buttons.

parameters.name: File / File Type
parameters.description: Declarations for handling file input and output inside the app, including allowed extensions.

parameters.name: Unit Set
parameters.description: Set of display units so an app can present results in the end user's preferred unit system.

tools.notes: Global declarations live under Applications > <app> > Declarations; forms can also carry local declarations, which are limited to Scalar, Array 1D, Array 2D and Choice List. Declarations are not model parameters - to influence the physics you still have to push their values into model.param() from a method or bind the form object directly to the parameter.

tools.name: Events
tools.description: Nodes that run a method automatically when something happens in the application instead of when a button is pressed. Global events fire on application startup and shutdown, or when the value of a declared variable or a model parameter changes; a Timer node fires repeatedly at a chosen interval. Use startup events to initialise state and load defaults, data-change events to keep dependent fields consistent, and timers for digital-twin apps that poll a sensor, database or web service.
tools.usage: Application Builder > Events > right-click > Event (or Timer); on a form object use its Settings window > Events section to run a method on change

parameters.name: Source
parameters.description: The declared variable, parameter or object whose change triggers the event.

parameters.name: On startup / On shutdown
parameters.description: Global events run when the application opens or closes.

parameters.name: Timer
parameters.description: Interval, start/stop control and the method to run on each tick.

parameters.name: Run method
parameters.description: Which method is executed when the event fires.

tools.example:
Set up an app that refreshes itself every 10 seconds:
1. Application Builder > Events > right-click > Timer.
2. Set the interval to 10000 ms and pick the method readSensorAndSolve.
3. Add an On startup event that calls the same method once, so the first view is populated.
4. In readSensorAndSolve, update model.param(), run the study and call useGraphics() to redraw.
tools.notes: Timer events were introduced for automated app updates and are the basis of IoT/digital-twin style applications. Beware of re-entrancy: a timer that fires while a long solve is still running can queue up work - guard with a Boolean declaration used as a busy flag.

tools.name: Test Application
tools.description: Runs the application you are building in a separate window (or in a web browser) without leaving the Application Builder, so you can click through the interface, check bindings and watch methods execute against the real model. Testing in the browser shows what users will see when the app is served from COMSOL Server. Because the test session uses the live model, any state it changes is kept - re-test from a saved copy when that matters.
tools.usage: Application Builder ribbon > Test Application (or Test in Web Browser)

parameters.name: Test Application
parameters.description: Launches the app in a desktop window using the current, unsaved definition.

parameters.name: Test in Web Browser
parameters.description: Launches the app in a chosen installed browser to preview the COMSOL Server look and feel.

parameters.name: Debug Log / Stop
parameters.description: Developer-tab tools for tracing method execution and halting a running test.

tools.example:
Typical build-test loop:
1. Edit a form or method in the Application Builder.
2. Click Test Application and exercise the input that changed.
3. Use Developer > Debug Log and message() calls in methods to trace values.
4. When satisfied, File > Save As to store the app in the .mph, or Compile Application to produce a standalone executable.
tools.notes: Deployment beyond testing needs an add-on: COMSOL Compiler turns the app into a standalone Windows, Linux or macOS executable that runs with no COMSOL licence (with optional password, expiry date and host-id lock), while COMSOL Server hosts apps for browser or COMSOL Client access with user management and version control. Apps that need a LiveLink product for CAD must be run through the COMSOL Client for Windows rather than a browser.

tools.name: ModelUtil.create
tools.description: Creates a new, empty model object in the COMSOL session and registers it under a tag, returning the Model handle that every other API call hangs off. It is the first line of essentially every COMSOL API for Java program and of every .java file produced by File > Save As > Model File for Java. Pair it with ModelUtil.remove to free the model when a script finishes, especially in loops that build many models.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Name the model is registered under in the session, e.g. "Model"; used by ModelUtil.remove and ModelUtil.tags().

parameters.name: ModelUtil.remove(tag)
parameters.description: Removes that model from memory.

parameters.name: ModelUtil.clear()
parameters.description: Removes all models from the session.

parameters.name: ModelUtil.initStandalone(boolean)
parameters.description: Starts a standalone COMSOL session from a plain Java program instead of connecting to a server.

parameters.name: ModelUtil.connect(host, port) / ModelUtil.disconnect()
parameters.description: Attach a client to a running COMSOL Multiphysics Server.

tools.notes: Run the resulting file with `comsol batch -inputfile Bar.java` (compiles and executes in one step) or compile first with `comsol compile`. Forgetting ModelUtil.remove in a long-running MATLAB or Python session is the most common cause of creeping memory use.

tools.name: ModelUtil.load
tools.description: Loads an existing .mph file into the session and returns the Model handle, registering it under the given tag. This is the entry point for scripts that modify or post-process a model somebody else built, as opposed to generating one from scratch. Everything afterwards - parameter changes, re-solving, evaluation, export - works on the returned object exactly as if the model had been created in code.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Session tag for the loaded model.

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Path to the .mph file (or a Model Manager database location when licensed).

parameters.name: ModelUtil.tags()
parameters.description: Lists the tags of all models currently in the session.

parameters.name: model.save(path)
parameters.description: Writes the model back out, optionally under a new name.

tools.notes: In LiveLink for MATLAB use mphload/mphopen instead, and in MPh for Python use client.load(); all three end up calling the same Java routine. Model files carry their version - loading a model saved by a newer COMSOL release will fail, so keep batch nodes and the authoring desktop on the same version.

tools.name: model.param().set
tools.description: Sets a global parameter's value (and optionally its description) in the model's Parameters table. Because geometry dimensions, material properties, boundary conditions and mesh sizes are normally written in terms of parameters, this single call is how external scripts drive a design study: change a parameter, rebuild, re-solve, evaluate. Values are strings so they can carry units and expressions, e.g. "2*L+1[mm]".

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Parameter name as it appears in Global Definitions > Parameters.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: String expression with an optional unit, e.g. "1[cm]" or "2*w".

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: Optional text shown in the Description column.

parameters.name: model.param().evaluate(name)
parameters.description: Returns the numeric value of a parameter after unit evaluation.

parameters.name: model.param(<ptag>)
parameters.description: Addresses a named parameter case / parameter group other than the default one.

tools.notes: Changing a parameter does not rebuild anything by itself - run the geometry, the mesh and the study explicitly, or COMSOL will solve on stale data. From the command line the same override is done without editing the model with `-pname L,w -plist 12[cm],1.2[cm]`, or with a parameter file via `-paramfile`.

tools.name: model.component().create
tools.description: Creates a Component - the container that owns a geometry, its definitions, materials, physics interfaces and mesh. Everything space-dependent in the API is addressed through it: model.component("comp1").geom(...), .physics(...), .material(...), .mesh(...). Building a model from source is essentially a sequence of create() calls on these sub-branches followed by run() on the geometry and mesh.

parameters.name: ctag
parameters.description: Component tag, conventionally "comp1".

parameters.name: geomDefault
parameters.description: true to add the default definitions/views a GUI component gets.

parameters.name: .geom().create(tag, sdim)
parameters.description: Creates a geometry sequence of space dimension 1, 2 or 3 (use geom.axisymmetric(true) for 2D axisymmetric).

parameters.name: .physics().create(tag, type, geomtag)
parameters.description: Adds a physics interface, e.g. "HeatTransfer", "SolidMechanics", "ElectricCurrents".

parameters.name: .material().create(tag)
parameters.description: Adds a material; property groups are filled with .propertyGroup("def").set(...).

parameters.name: .mesh().create(tag)
parameters.description: Adds a mesh sequence; autoMeshSize(n) picks a predefined element size, 1 = extremely fine ... 9 = extremely coarse.

tools.notes: geom().run() builds the whole sequence; geom().run(<ftag>) builds up to one feature, which is useful for debugging a failing operation. Physics and material type strings are long and version-specific - the reliable way to get them is to build the node in the GUI and read the generated code with File > Save As > Model File for Java.

tools.name: model.study().run
tools.description: Solves a study: generates the solver sequence if needed, runs every enabled study step in order, and stores the solution. This is the call that actually computes, and it is what a batch script invokes after setting parameters and rebuilding geometry and mesh. For finer control, generate the sequence explicitly with model.sol().createAutoSequence(<studytag>) and then drive the solver node yourself with model.sol(<soltag>).runAll().

parameters.name: studytag
parameters.description: Study tag such as "std1"; visible in the Model Builder with Model Tree Node Text > Tag, or via model.study().tags().

parameters.name: model.study(tag).create(steptag, type)
parameters.description: Adds a study step: "Stationary", "Transient", "Frequency", "Eigenfrequency", "Parametric", ...

parameters.name: model.sol().createAutoSequence(studytag)
parameters.description: Builds the default solver sequence for that study without solving.

parameters.name: model.sol(soltag).runAll()
parameters.description: Runs the whole solver sequence; runFromTo() runs part of it.

parameters.name: model.batch(...)
parameters.description: Job configurations: Batch, Batch Sweep, Cluster Computing and Cluster Sweep nodes.

tools.notes: study().run() regenerates the solver sequence when the model has changed, which can silently discard manual solver tweaks; when you have hand-tuned a solver node, call model.sol("sol1").runAll() instead. A long study in a batch job should be paired with -batchlog so the solver log survives, and -recover lets an interrupted run restart from the last stored solution.

tools.name: model.save
tools.description: Writes the model - tree, settings, mesh and (unless cleared) the solution - to a file. Called with just a path it saves a .mph; COMSOL also uses the extension to write the model as source code, which is how a session becomes a reusable script. Saving after a batch solve is what makes the results available to a later postprocessing run.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Target file path; .mph for a model file.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Alternative output: a Java model file (.java), a MATLAB model file (.m) or a VBA model file (.vba).

parameters.name: model.resetHist() / Compact History
parameters.description: Discards the recorded modelling history so the saved source contains only the calls needed to rebuild the final state.

parameters.name: model.mesh().clearMeshes() / model.sol().clearSolution()
parameters.description: Shrink the file by dropping mesh or solution data before saving.

tools.notes: In the GUI the same thing is File > Save As with file type 'Model File for Java' (or for MATLAB / VBA); run Compact History first (Developer ribbon) so the generated file contains the final model rather than every experiment. Generated .java files can be run directly with `comsol batch -inputfile Model.java`.

tools.name: mphstart
tools.description: Connects a MATLAB session to a running COMSOL Multiphysics Server and adds the COMSOL Java classes to the MATLAB class path, so that LiveLink for MATLAB functions and the model object become available. Use it when MATLAB was started on its own; if you start the pair with `comsol mphserver matlab` the connection is made for you. After mphstart succeeds you can import com.comsol.model.util.* and work with model objects exactly as in Java.
tools.usage: mphstart  |  mphstart(port)  |  mphstart(host, port)  |  mphstart(host, port, user, password)

parameters.name: port
parameters.description: TCP port the COMSOL Multiphysics Server listens on (2036 by default).

parameters.name: host
parameters.description: Host name or IP address of the machine running the server.

parameters.name: user / password
parameters.description: Credentials when the server requires login.

parameters.name: mphversion
parameters.description: Companion function returning the COMSOL version MATLAB is connected to.

tools.notes: Start the server first with `comsol server -port 2036` (Windows: comsolmphserver). mphlaunch opens the COMSOL Desktop against the same server session so you can look at the model you are scripting. Remember ModelUtil.remove('Model') when you are done to release the model from the server.

tools.name: mphload
tools.description: Loads a COMSOL .mph file into MATLAB and returns the model object, which is the Java Model handle wrapped for MATLAB syntax. From there every API call works with dots instead of parentheses-and-semicolons: model.param.set(...), model.study('std1').run(). This is the starting point of virtually every LiveLink for MATLAB script that works on an existing model.

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Path to the .mph file; the extension may be omitted.

parameters.name: modeltag
parameters.description: Tag to register the model under in the server session (default 'Model').

parameters.name: mphopen
parameters.description: Sibling function that loads a model and can also open a file dialog or a model from the Application Libraries.

parameters.name: mphsave
parameters.description: Writes the model back to file: mphsave(model, filename).

tools.notes: Other model-level helpers: mphmodel to print the model structure, mphtags to list node tags, mphgeom and mphmesh to draw the geometry and mesh in a MATLAB figure, mphplot to reproduce a COMSOL plot group, mphselectbox / mphselectball / mphselectcoords to find entity numbers by coordinates, and mphgetexpressions to list the variables defined on a node.

tools.name: mpheval
tools.description: Evaluates one or more expressions at the mesh node points of a selection and returns a structure containing the values, the point coordinates, the element connectivity and the units. Unlike a Derived Value it hands you the raw field, so MATLAB can do the reduction - fitting, filtering, custom plotting, error norms against an analytic solution. It is the workhorse for getting a whole solution out of COMSOL and into MATLAB arrays.

parameters.name: expressions
parameters.description: Cell array (or single string) of COMSOL expressions to evaluate.

parameters.name: edim
parameters.description: Element dimension: 'domain', 'boundary', 'edge' or 'point'.

parameters.name: selection
parameters.description: Entity numbers or a named selection limiting where the evaluation happens.

parameters.name: dataset
parameters.description: Dataset tag to evaluate on (defaults to the active solution dataset).

parameters.name: t / solnum / outersolnum
parameters.description: Time, inner solution number and outer (sweep) solution number to evaluate at.

tools.notes: Returned fields include expr, p (points), t (elements), ve (vertex indices), d1..dn (data per expression) and unit. mpheval samples mesh nodes; use mphinterp when you need values at coordinates you choose yourself, and mphmean / mphmax / mphmin for quick scalar reductions.

tools.name: mphinterp
tools.description: Evaluates expressions at arbitrary coordinates you supply, interpolating the finite-element solution, or at the points of a given dataset. Use it to sample along a path, on a regular grid for comparison with measurements, or at scattered sensor positions - no Cut Point or Cut Line dataset needs to exist in the model. It also returns the unit of the result when you ask for an extra output argument.

parameters.name: coord
parameters.description: Double matrix whose COLUMNS are the evaluation coordinates (transpose row-wise data before passing it).

parameters.name: dataset
parameters.description: Dataset tag; coordinate-based evaluation is only supported on Solution datasets.

parameters.name: edim
parameters.description: Dimension the expressions are evaluated in - 'domain', 'boundary', 'edge', 'point'; points are projected onto the closest entity of that dimension.

parameters.name: coorderr
parameters.description: 'on' (default) raises an error if all coordinates fall outside the geometry.

parameters.name: t / solnum / outersolnum / unit
parameters.description: Time, solution numbers and output unit for the evaluation.

tools.notes: The most common mistake is passing coordinates row-wise: mphinterp expects one column per point. Coordinates outside the geometry return NaN (or an error, depending on coorderr). The expression may be any valid COMSOL expression, not just a dependent variable.

tools.name: mphint2
tools.description: Integrates expressions over selected lines, surfaces or volumes and returns the values to MATLAB, without adding a Derived Values node to the model. Use it for total flux, total force, stored energy, flow rate or any other extensive quantity you want directly as a MATLAB number, including across a whole time series or parameter sweep in one call. The optional second output gives the unit of the integral.

parameters.name: edim
parameters.description: Integration dimension: 'line', 'surface', 'volume', or the integer 1, 2 or 3.

parameters.name: selection
parameters.description: Entity numbers or a named selection; defaults to all.

parameters.name: intorder
parameters.description: Integration order, default 4 - raise it for high-order or oscillatory integrands.

parameters.name: intvolume / intsurface
parameters.description: 'on' to revolve a 2D axisymmetric integral into a true volume or surface integral.

parameters.name: dataseries
parameters.description: Optional reduction over the solution series: average, integral, maximum, rms, stddev or variance.

tools.notes: Results come back as an M-by-P matrix: M inner solutions (time steps) by P outer solutions (sweep values), so a transient integral is returned as a whole history. Companions: mphmean for averages, mphmax / mphmin for extrema, and mphglobal for expressions that need no spatial selection.

tools.name: mphglobal
tools.description: Evaluates global expressions - parameters, global variables and lumped physics quantities such as terminal current, total force, eigenfrequency or a probe - and returns them to MATLAB as a numeric array with one entry per solution. It is the quickest way to pull a sweep's key output into MATLAB for plotting, curve fitting or optimisation, since no selection or dataset construction is needed.

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Global expression or cell array of expressions.

parameters.name: dataset
parameters.description: Dataset tag; for a parametric sweep this selects which sweep solution supplies the rows.

parameters.name: solnum / outersolnum
parameters.description: Which inner (time/eigenvalue) and outer (sweep) solution numbers to return.

parameters.name: unit
parameters.description: Unit to return the values in.

parameters.name: dataseries
parameters.description: Optional reduction over the solution series.

tools.notes: For a frequency or parametric sweep the returned vector is ordered by solution number, and mphglobal(model,'freq') or the sweep parameter gives you the matching abscissa. Use mphtable(model, 'tbl1') to read a table a Derived Value or Evaluation Group has already filled, and mphsolinfo / mphsolutioninfo to inspect what solutions exist.

tools.name: mphnavigator
tools.description: Opens an interactive browser over the model object: the tree of nodes with their tags, the properties of the selected node and the Java methods available on it, plus tools for copying the matching API code to the clipboard. It is the fastest way to discover the property name or type string you need for a node you built in the GUI, and to work out how to loop over a node's children. Practically indispensable when writing LiveLink for MATLAB scripts against an unfamiliar model.

parameters.name: model
parameters.description: Model object to browse; with no argument the function uses the model in the workspace.

parameters.name: Properties / Methods panels
parameters.description: Show the selected node's property values and the Java methods you can call on it.

parameters.name: Tools > copy code
parameters.description: Copies the API call for the selected node, including a 'copy code: loop' variant that iterates over its children.

parameters.name: Tools > Solutions
parameters.description: Overview of studies, solutions, datasets and sweeps in the model.

tools.notes: mphsearch is the companion dialog for searching the model object and the COMSOL API documentation by keyword. The modern App Designer based interfaces for mphnavigator, mphopen and mphsearch need MATLAB R2020a or later; the legacy interfaces still work on older releases.

tools.name: mph.start
tools.description: Starts a local COMSOL session from Python using the MPh package and returns a Client object that owns the models. MPh talks to the same COMSOL Java API through JPype, so anything the Java API can do is reachable, while the common tasks get a pythonic wrapper. Only one client can exist per Python process, which is why parallel sweeps are normally done with one process per worker.

parameters.name: cores
parameters.description: Limit the number of threads COMSOL uses; by default all cores are used.

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: Pick a specific installed COMSOL version, e.g. version='6.3'; the newest one is used by default.

parameters.name: port
parameters.description: Server port for client-server mode; 0 (default) lets the server choose a free port.

parameters.name: client.create(name=None)
parameters.description: Creates a new empty model.

parameters.name: client.remove(model) / client.clear()
parameters.description: Frees one model or all models held in memory.

parameters.name: client.modules()
parameters.description: Lists the licensed add-on products available to this session.

tools.example:
import mph
client = mph.start(cores=4)
model = client.create('demo')
model.create('geometries', 3)
model.create('geometries/Geometry 1', 'Block')
model.property('geometries/Geometry 1/Block 1', 'size', ('0.1', '0.2', '0.5'))
model.build('Geometry 1')
model.save('demo.mph')
client.remove(model)
tools.notes: MPh is an open-source community package, not a COMSOL product - install it with `pip install MPh`. client.connect(port, host) attaches to an already running COMSOL Multiphysics Server instead of starting one locally, and client.caching(True) keeps loaded models in memory across repeated loads.

tools.name: client.load
tools.description: Loads a .mph file (or a Model Manager database URI) and returns an MPh Model object wrapping the COMSOL model. The Model class is deliberately focused on inspecting an existing model, changing parameters, solving and evaluating results rather than authoring models from scratch - although model.create() and model.property() do cover structural edits, and model.java drops you into the full Java API whenever the wrapper is not enough.

parameters.name: file
parameters.description: Path to the .mph file, or a Model Manager database location.

parameters.name: client.models() / names() / files()
parameters.description: Lists the models held in memory, their names and their file paths.

parameters.name: model.java
parameters.description: The underlying COMSOL Java model object, for any call MPh does not wrap.

parameters.name: model.geometries() / physics() / materials() / meshes() / studies() / plots() / exports()
parameters.description: Inspection helpers returning the names of the corresponding nodes.

tools.example:
import mph
client = mph.start()
model = client.load('busbar.mph')
print(model.name(), model.version())
print(model.parameters())
print(model.studies(), model.exports())
tools.notes: Node paths in MPh are strings such as 'geometries/Geometry 1/Block 1' or 'physics/Electric Currents', using the node labels shown in the Model Builder rather than the Java tags. model.clear() drops stored solution, mesh and plot data (handy before saving a small file) and model.reset() discards the modelling history.

tools.name: model.solve
tools.description: Runs a study in an MPh model, either a named study or (with no argument) the model's default study sequence. Combined with model.parameter() this gives a three-line parameter sweep in Python: set a parameter, solve, evaluate. Use model.build() and model.mesh() first when the change affects geometry or meshing, and model.save() afterwards if the solved state should be kept.

parameters.name: study
parameters.description: Name of the study to run, e.g. 'Study 1' or a custom label; omit to run the default.

parameters.name: model.parameter(name, value=None, *, evaluate=False)
parameters.description: Reads or sets one global parameter; pass evaluate=True to get a number rather than the expression string.

parameters.name: model.parameters(evaluate=False)
parameters.description: Returns all global parameters as a mapping.

parameters.name: model.build(geometry=None)
parameters.description: Builds a geometry sequence.

parameters.name: model.mesh(mesh=None)
parameters.description: Builds a mesh sequence.

tools.example:
import mph
client = mph.start(cores=1)
model = client.load('capacitor.mph')
for d in (1.0, 1.5, 2.0):
    model.parameter('d', f'{d}[mm]')
    model.solve('static')
    C = model.evaluate('2*es.intWe/U^2', 'pF')
    print(f'd = {d} mm -> C = {C:.3f} pF')
model.save('capacitor_swept.mph')
tools.notes: A solve raises a Python exception if COMSOL reports a solver error, so wrap sweeps in try/except when some parameter values are expected to fail. Because only one client exists per process, run parallel sweeps with multiprocessing - one mph.start(cores=1) client per worker process.

tools.name: model.evaluate
tools.description: Evaluates a COMSOL expression (or list of expressions) on a solved MPh model and returns NumPy arrays - a scalar for a global quantity, a field array for a space-dependent one, and a tuple when several expressions are requested. It is the main way results leave COMSOL for Python analysis with NumPy, pandas or Matplotlib, and it accepts a unit so the numbers come back in whatever units you want.
tools.usage: value = model.evaluate(expression, unit=None, dataset=None, inner=None, outer=None)

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: COMSOL expression or list of expressions, e.g. 'T' or ['x','y','z','T'].

parameters.name: unit
parameters.description: Unit for the returned values, e.g. 'degC', 'pF', 'W'.

parameters.name: dataset
parameters.description: Dataset name to evaluate on; defaults to the model's default dataset.

parameters.name: inner
parameters.description: Inner solution selection - time step or eigenvalue index, or 'first'/'last'.

parameters.name: outer
parameters.description: Outer solution selection for a parametric sweep.

tools.example:
import mph
client = mph.start()
model = client.load('busbar.mph')
model.solve()
(x, y, z, T) = model.evaluate(['x', 'y', 'z', 'T'])
imax = T.argmax()
print(f'Tmax = {T.max():.2f} K at ({x[imax]:.4f}, {y[imax]:.4f}, {z[imax]:.4f})')
model.export('Data 1', 'field.txt')
model.save('busbar_out.mph')
tools.notes: The values match exactly what the corresponding table shows in the GUI. model.export(node=None, file=None) runs one export node - or, with no arguments, every export node in the model using its stored filenames - and model.save(path, format) can also write 'Java', 'Matlab' or 'VBA' source instead of a .mph. There is no wrapper for reading a COMSOL table directly; reach through model.java for that.

tools.name: comsol batch
tools.description: Runs COMSOL without a graphical user interface: loads a .mph (or a compiled Java model file), optionally overrides parameters, solves a chosen study, runs export nodes and methods, and writes the result to a new file. This is the standard entry point for cluster and queue submission, overnight parameter studies and CI-style regression runs. On Windows the same program is called comsolbatch (comsolbatch.exe).

parameters.name: -inputfile / -outputfile
parameters.description: Model to run and where to write the solved model; without -outputfile the input file is overwritten.

parameters.name: -study / -job
parameters.description: Tag of the study to compute, or of the batch job configuration to run.

parameters.name: -pname / -plist
parameters.description: Comma-separated parameter names and matching values to override before solving.

parameters.name: -paramfile
parameters.description: File of parameter names (first row) and value tuples (following rows) for a file-driven sweep.

parameters.name: -methodcall / -nosave
parameters.description: Run a model method by name; -nosave skips writing the model back out.

parameters.name: -batchlog / -recover / -alivetime
parameters.description: Log file for the run, restart from the last stored solution, and the keep-alive timeout.

parameters.name: -np / -nn / -nnhost / -f
parameters.description: Shared-memory cores, total MPI processes, processes per host, and the host file for cluster runs.

parameters.name: -graphics / -createplots
parameters.description: Start with graphics libraries so plot groups, image and animation exports can be rendered.

tools.example:
# Solve one study with two overridden parameters on 8 cores, logging to file
comsol -np 8 batch -inputfile busbar.mph -outputfile busbar_out.mph \
       -study std1 -pname L,Vtot -plist 12[cm],20[mV] -batchlog run.log

# Run a Java model file directly, and a model method on an existing model
comsol batch -inputfile BuildModel.java -outputfile model.mph
comsolbatch -inputfile my_file.mph -methodcall my_method -nosave
tools.notes: Study tags are shown by enabling Model Tree Node Text > Tag in the Model Builder. Batch Sweep nodes cannot be launched from the command line - drive a sweep with -pname/-plist or -paramfile instead. Parameter values containing brackets normally need quoting in the shell.

tools.name: comsol server
tools.description: Starts a COMSOL Multiphysics Server: a headless COMSOL process that holds models in memory and accepts connections from LiveLink clients over TCP. LiveLink for MATLAB (mphstart), MPh for Python and plain Java clients all attach to it, and the full COMSOL Desktop can run as a thin client against it. Use it to put the solver on a big machine while the user interface or script runs somewhere else.
tools.usage: comsol server [-port <port>] [-silent]   (Windows: comsolmphserver; MATLAB in one step: comsol mphserver matlab)

parameters.name: -port
parameters.description: TCP port to listen on; 2036 is the conventional default.

parameters.name: -silent
parameters.description: Suppress interactive prompts, for use in scripts and services.

parameters.name: -np
parameters.description: Number of cores the server may use.

parameters.name: comsol mphserver matlab
parameters.description: Starts the server and a MATLAB session already connected to it.

parameters.name: comsol client
parameters.description: Runs the COMSOL Desktop as a client against a running server.

tools.example:
# Terminal 1: start the server
comsol server -port 2036 -silent

# Terminal 2: connect from MATLAB
matlab -r "mphstart(2036); model = mphload('busbar.mph'); model.study('std1').run()"

# ...or from Python
python -c "import mph; c = mph.Client(); c.connect(2036); print(c.modules())"
tools.notes: Do not confuse this with COMSOL Server, the separate licensed product for hosting Application Builder apps to browsers and the COMSOL Client. A server holds models until they are removed - call ModelUtil.remove / client.remove when a script finishes, or long-lived servers grow without bound.

tools.name: comsol compile
tools.description: Compiles a COMSOL API model file for Java into a .class file that comsol batch can run without recompiling, using the JDK bundled with COMSOL. Use it when a Java model file is executed repeatedly, when you want compilation errors reported before a queued job starts, or when building a library of model-generating classes. On Windows the program is called comsolcompile.

parameters.name: <ModelFile.java>
parameters.description: COMSOL API for Java source file, normally produced by File > Save As > Model File for Java.

parameters.name: output
parameters.description: A .class file beside the source, runnable with `comsol batch -inputfile ModelFile.class`.

parameters.name: comsol -open / -run / -edit
parameters.description: Open, run or edit an application .mph from the command line.

tools.example:
# Compile once, then run the compiled model repeatedly
comsol compile BuildBusbar.java
comsol batch -inputfile BuildBusbar.class -outputfile busbar.mph

# comsol batch can also compile and run a .java file in one step
comsol batch -inputfile BuildBusbar.java -outputfile busbar.mph
tools.notes: This is not the same thing as COMSOL Compiler, the add-on product that turns an Application Builder app into a standalone executable for Windows, Linux and macOS that runs with no COMSOL licence - that compilation is started from the Application Builder ribbon. Java model files must be compiled against the same COMSOL version they will run on.
